To override something means to use your authority, power, or position to step in, cancel what was already in place, and replace it with something else — your own decision, setting, or action.

Think of it this way: something is already happening, already decided, or already set. Then someone (or something) with greater power comes along and says, "No. Disregard that. We're doing it my way now." That act of stepping in and taking control is overriding.

Two things are always involved:

  1. Something already in place — a decision, a setting, a rule, a system, an instinct.
  2. A person or force with enough authority to set that thing aside.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

Override is not just about cancelling something. It is about substituting something. When you override, you don't leave a blank — you replace what was there with your own version. And the thing being overridden doesn't disappear forever. It was just not allowed to operate in this particular situation.

Also crucial: override implies a hierarchy. The thing doing the overriding must hold more power than the thing being overridden. A junior employee cannot override the CEO's decision. But the CEO can override the junior employee's decision. There is always a difference in rank, authority, or strength between the two sides.

The word is used across many different situations. Here are the main ones:

1. Authority and Decisions

When someone in power rejects or reverses a decision made by someone below them — or by a group — they override it.

  • A doctor recommends a treatment, but the hospital administration overrides that recommendation and mandates a different protocol.
  • A committee votes to approve a project, but the director overrides their vote and cancels it.
  • In many governments, a president or monarch can override a law passed by parliament by vetoing it.

In all these cases, the higher authority steps in and their decision takes the place of the one that came before it.

2. Rules and Normal Procedures

Sometimes, in special circumstances, a rule or normal process is overridden — meaning it is set aside because something more urgent or more powerful demands it.

  • During an emergency, the government declared that certain privacy laws would be overridden to allow faster data sharing between hospitals.
  • The terms of the contract override anything we agreed to verbally — meaning the written contract takes precedence and cancels out anything said aloud.

Here, "override" tells you which rule or agreement wins when two are in conflict.

3. Machines, Systems, and Technology

Machines and automated systems often have built-in behaviours — things they do automatically or by default. A human (or another system) can override those automatic behaviours by taking manual control.

  • A pilot can override the plane's autopilot and fly it manually.
  • You can override your car's parking sensors — ignoring their alert and proceeding anyway.
  • In a factory, a safety system might automatically shut down a machine. An engineer can override that shutdown if they determine it was a false alarm.
  • On your phone or computer, a default setting (like "auto-brightness") can be overridden when you manually set the brightness yourself — your manual setting takes priority over the automatic one.

The key feeling here: the machine would have done one thing, but a human (or a higher system) stepped in and forced it to do something different instead.

4. In Software and Programming

In programming, especially in object-oriented languages, override has a very specific technical meaning, though it follows the same general logic.

When you build a program, you often use templates or blueprints called "classes." A child class (a more specific version) can override a method (a function/behaviour) it inherited from a parent class (a more general version). This means the child class says: "Yes, I inherited this behaviour from my parent, but I'm replacing it with my own version. Use mine instead."

  • The parent class has a method called speak() which makes a generic sound. The child class Dog overrides speak() to bark. Now, whenever a Dog object speaks, it uses the Dog's version — not the parent's.

Same logic: something in place is replaced by something with more specific or higher authority.

5. Emotions, Instincts, and Inner States

Interestingly, "override" is also used when one feeling or force within a person is so strong that it suppresses or cancels another.

  • Her determination overrode her fear. (Her determination was so powerful that it cancelled out the fear — the fear was there, but it was not allowed to control her actions.)
  • Exhaustion finally overrode his will to keep going. (His exhaustion became stronger than his willpower, and it took control.)
  • His professional duty overrode his personal feelings.

Notice the same structure: one force is stronger and takes command over the other.
What "Override" Feels Like in Any Sentence

Whenever you see or hear the word "override," ask yourself:

  • What was already in place? (The decision, the rule, the setting, the behaviour, the feeling.)
  • Who or what stepped in? (The higher authority, the stronger force.)
  • What replaced it? (The new decision, the manual control, the stronger emotion.)

That three-part logic is always present.

• The manager overrode the team's decision.

(The team decided something; the manager cancelled it and imposed a different one.)

  • His hunger overrode all other thoughts.

(Hunger became so dominant that it pushed everything else out.)

  • You can override the default settings.

(You can replace the automatic/preset settings with your own choices.)

  • The Supreme Court overrode the lower court's ruling.

(A higher legal authority cancelled the lower court's decision and replaced it with its own.)

  • The automatic system was overridden manually.

(A human stepped in and took control away from the automatic system.)

"Override" carries a sense of asserting dominance or authority in a deliberate way. It is rarely accidental. When something is overridden, there is an active, intentional act of one force using its superior position to set aside what was previously in control. It can sometimes feel forceful or even confrontational — especially in human relationships — because it means one person's judgment is being explicitly set aside in favour of another's.

It is a powerful word. It signals that something did not get to stand on its own — something stronger intervened.
